items.text: The registrar account requires multi-factor authentication, and the account's recovery contacts are current and controlled by the organization.
Transfer lock is enabled on every domain the organization owns.
Registry lock is enabled where the registry offers it, so the domain cannot be changed until the lock is removed.
Auto-renew is enabled on every domain, and the payment method on file at the registrar is current.
The organization keeps an inventory of every domain it owns, at every registrar, with a named owner and purpose for each.
The DNS provider account requires two-step verification, and access to it is limited to the administrators who manage the zone.
DNSSEC is enabled for every zone, and the DS records at the registrar match the zone's DNSKEY records.
The DNS provider keeps an audit log of zone changes, and changes are reviewed against the changes the organization intended to make.
Every zone's delegation is clean: the parent's nameserver records match the zone's own, with no lame or stale delegations.
Every zone is served by at least two authoritative nameservers on separate networks, so one network or provider failure does not take the domain down.
Zone transfers (AXFR) are restricted to the organization's own secondary servers; the zone cannot be transferred by an outside party.
A current copy of every zone's records is kept under the organization's own control (as records-as-code or an export), so the zone can be rebuilt at another provider.
Exactly one SPF record is published for each sending domain, it names only services that still send for the domain, and it stays within the ten-lookup limit.
The SPF record ends in a hard fail (-all); a soft fail (~all) appears only as a dated step on the way to enforcement.
Every service that sends mail for the domain signs with DKIM, using keys of at least 2048 bits.

A DMARC record is published for every domain, with an enforcement policy in force (p=quarantine or p=reject). Monitoring only (p=none) appears only as a dated step toward enforcement, and p=reject is adopted only after aggregate reports show it will not break the domain's mailing-list or forwarded mail.
DMARC aggregate reports go to a mailbox or service that is actually reviewed, and senders the reports show as misaligned are fixed or removed.
Subdomain policy is set deliberately: the subdomain policy (sp) and the non-existent subdomain policy (np) are published, not left to defaults.
Domains that send no mail publish a null SPF record (v=spf1 -all) and a DMARC record at reject, so they cannot be spoofed.
Every SPF include and every DKIM selector in the zone maps to a sending service the organization still uses; the mapping is re-checked at least quarterly.
An MTA-STS policy is published for each mail domain and set to enforce, with the policy file served over HTTPS.
An SMTP TLS reporting (TLS-RPT) record publishes a reporting address that is monitored.
CAA records name the certificate authorities allowed to issue certificates for the domain, and no others.
Where the mail platform supports DANE, TLSA records are published for the mail servers and kept in step with certificate changes.
The organization keeps an inventory of its subdomains and what each one points at; an unknown subdomain is investigated, not ignored.
No CNAME record points at a service the organization no longer uses; dangling records to deprovisioned services are removed.
Delegations of subdomains to third parties are inventoried with a named owner and reviewed at least quarterly.
Wildcard DNS records exist only where a named service needs them, and each wildcard is recorded with its reason.

title: DNS and Registrar — Domain Security Expected State (curated)
